overview: The Bureau of Reclamation, part of the Interior Department, runs dams, canals and reservoirs across the western United States. Under current law, private companies, utilities and other non-federal groups can lease the right to generate hydropower at some of these sites, but mainly at small canals and pipelines (called conduits) and for certain pumped storage projects. This bill expands that leasing option to hydropower at all Bureau of Reclamation facilities, and treats power generation as secondary to the facilities' water-supply purposes. It also sorts out which agency is in charge: existing permits from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the agency that licenses most hydropower, stay in place while active, after which the Bureau alone has jurisdiction over the site. The bill says it does not expand leasing authority outside a project's boundaries. As of August 27, 2026, it had been approved by a House committee and placed on the House calendar for possible floor action.
for: Supporters say letting non-federal developers add hydropower at existing federal water facilities would produce more clean electricity and rural jobs without building new dams.
against: Critics say widening private power development at public water projects could complicate water management and blur oversight, especially as jurisdiction shifts from federal energy regulators to the Bureau of Reclamation.
